The idea that technology companies don't pay dividends comes from the industry's early years, when most businesses focused on growing as quickly as possible. During the dot-com boom of the late 1990s and early 2000s, tech companies typically reinvested their profits into expansion, new products, and gaining market share. Returning cash to shareholders was rarely a priority. Over time, this created the perception that technology stocks were not suitable for dividend investors.

That perception has started to change as the industry has matured. Several major tech companies have introduced dividend payments to reward shareholders. 2024 was an important year in this shift, with some of the biggest names in technology announcing dividend policies. Most of these stocks still offer modest yields, but their ability to grow payouts as earnings increase makes them worth considering for long-term dividend investors. It also gives dividend growth portfolios greater exposure to a sector that has traditionally been underrepresented.

Also read: 10 Best Dividend Stocks for Long Term Growth

Technology stocks have played a major role in driving market returns in recent years, and dividend investing is beginning to reflect that shift. Analysts believe this creates new opportunities for both investors and companies. Matt Quinlan, lead portfolio manager for Franklin Equity Income fund and Franklin Rising Dividends fund, said income strategies now "have access and exposure to those names that have driven the market more recently." Tom Huber, portfolio manager for T. Rowe Price Dividend Growth fund, also sees room for this trend to continue. "There will be more and more opportunities for dividend growth investors to buy technology stocks," he says.

Most technology companies still prefer to use their cash to grow the business or buy back shares rather than distribute it through dividends. That's been the norm for years. The decision by some of the largest tech companies to start paying dividends shows that this approach is gradually changing. Quinlan said that these companies have attractive financial models that generate tremendous cash flow. They can both invest in the business and reinvest to maintain those competitive positions, while also paying dividends. Billionaire investors basically pick them for the first reason. The yield on these stocks is not as attractive for billionaire investors; the main reason is that they think these stocks can generate superior risk-adjusted returns over the long term.
